# CommonCurrent: Vision and Technical Horizons

Bounded repair after initial independent review · 2026-10-28 · Destination aspiration: roughly 2033

CommonCurrent should make dependable repair an ordinary option for essential household equipment, delivered by independent businesses whose skill earns a sustainable living. A household should be able to understand its options, authorize an affordable repair, and regain a working appliance without coordinating the repair industry itself. A technician should arrive with a credible parts plan and useful history, exercise accountable judgment, and be paid for skilled work rather than absorb the cost of preventable return visits.

Our chosen destination is a **repair coordination network owned in practice by the relationships it supports**: independent shops remain the service providers and owners of their records; CommonCurrent connects consented information, verified parts commitments and accountable handoffs across shops and suppliers. The ambition is broader than scheduling software. It is to make a dependable local repair service possible even when no single shop has every part, skill or available appointment.

This is a proposed direction, not a claim that the network exists or a promise of universal coverage. Every observation below comes from the [synthetic brief](../../evaluation-design/main-brief.md); its people, businesses and research are fictional. Numeric exit thresholds below are proposed decision criteria, not observed results or contractual guarantees.

## Why this future matters

People need a working refrigerator or washing machine, not a completed service ticket. Independent shops already bring local trust and practical skill, but coordinating parts and visits consumes time without reliably restoring that equipment sooner. Among 410 jobs logged by six shops, 96 required another visit and 54 of those recorded missing or incorrect parts (E2). That is evidence of a significant problem in this sample, not proof that parts coordination caused all repeats or that software could prevent them. Thirteen of eighteen interviewed owners called parts availability a major source of repeat visits; eleven expressed interest in paying more for dependable availability (E1). Neither statement establishes a purchase.

Nine of twelve households described disruption during repair waits, and four replaced an appliance (E3). We do not know whether those replacements were avoidable, affordable or environmentally worse. Technicians see their own risk: eight of ten worried about blame from uncertain advice, and six wanted a named human responsible for final diagnosis (E5). A service that improves dispatch statistics by transferring risk or unpaid work to technicians would fail this vision.

The pivotal hypothesis is that dependable repair requires **credible commitments between people**, as much as better information: which part is appropriate, who has actually reserved it, who will perform the work, what the household has authorized, and who takes responsibility when a commitment fails. CommonCurrent's existing relationships with 34 paying shops offer a starting place to test this hypothesis. They do not establish broad demand or a network advantage.

The opportunity is timely because we have a concrete coordination problem, a small installed base and a manual mechanism worth testing. In 31 concierge jobs, dispatchers reported six apparent avoided repeat visits, at a median 19 minutes of staff time per job (E4). Those unverified, uncontrolled results justify a bounded experiment. They do not justify expansion or claims of economic viability. No external market catalyst or comprehensive landscape evidence is available.

## A household can finish the repair, without becoming its project manager

An imagined 2033 experience: a household reports a failing refrigerator to its usual independent shop. With the household's permission, the shop sees relevant service history, including where confidence is low. A technician determines what must be inspected and remains responsible for diagnosis and safety decisions. CommonCurrent helps the dispatcher assemble a plan: a supplier confirms a specific part and reservation, the shop offers a feasible visit, and the household sees a price or explicit range, alternatives and the consequences of waiting. It can decline without losing access to its own records.

If the shop cannot meet the need, it can offer an accountable handoff to another participating shop. The household approves that handoff and the limited information it requires. If the reservation fails, the service surfaces that failure before an unnecessary visit where possible; a named person explains the revised options. A completed ticket is insufficient: the technician records the work and relevant professional judgment, and the household can report whether the appliance works and whether the problem returns. CommonCurrent never declares an appliance safe to operate.

Where repair is inappropriate or unaffordable, honest options and an orderly end to the episode still matter. Replacement is not automatically a failure; concealing its cost or pushing repeated low-value repairs is. Partnerships with housing providers, community organizations or assistance programs could fund access for households that otherwise defer essential repairs. Their incentives, consent practices and actual willingness to fund outcomes must be tested before they become part of the business.

Success would mean less disruption and avoidable expense, better earnings and working conditions for repairers, and fewer premature replacements where repair is appropriate. Avoided waste is a desired consequence requiring evidence; we cannot translate repaired jobs into disposal or emissions claims.

## The strategic choice

Three plausible futures lead to different products and obligations:

| Direction | Promise and attraction | Principal bet and sacrifice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Better operations software for each shop | Lower administrative effort; familiar buyers and distribution | Useful but insufficient to coordinate failures between organizations. Competes with an established, inexpensive alternative. |
| A household repair relationship for life | One place for continuity, advice and purchasing across appliances | Requires trust, repeat demand, household acquisition and service economics that the supplied evidence does not establish. It could displace existing shop relationships. |
| A repair coordination network serving independent shops and households | More dependable restoration through parts commitments and accountable local handoffs | Requires partner participation, enforceable service practices and viable coordination costs. Harder than a software feature, but closest to the observed friction and consequential household outcome. |

Choose the third. Preserve better shop operations as its usable entry point, and test household continuity as a possible later benefit. Do not adopt a household subscription as the organizing assumption. The founder's lifelong-relationship assertion remains plausible but unproven; household follow-up should examine whether continuity belongs with a shop, an appliance record, a property manager or CommonCurrent itself.

FleetDesk Lite already provides scheduling, invoicing, offline notes and export for $49 per shop per month. Spreadsheets, supplier phone reservations and technician relationships accomplish real coordination today; two owners prefer that combination for resilience and independence. CommonCurrent must demonstrate incremental reliability and net economic value against that combination, including the option of simply improving phone procedures. Integration alone is not a reason to switch. Doing nothing avoids migration and coordination fees, but leaves the sampled failure pattern unaddressed. If a low-cost checklist and better calls deliver the same benefit, we should support that method or stop building the proposed infrastructure.

Begin with parts-sensitive appliance repairs in a compact service area where participating shops and suppliers can make meaningful commitments. Recruit beyond today's customers when testing transferability. Expand into underserved households and complementary shops only where service capacity and sustainable access can be demonstrated. Density and dependable relationships matter more than total account count.

We deliberately exclude autonomous diagnosis or dispatch, software-issued safety clearance, compulsory pooling of shop records, sale of identifiable household information and a platform that competes with shops for their customers. We also decline an immediate nationwide availability promise. These choices sacrifice some growth speed and automation savings to preserve accountability and viable independent businesses. They do not limit the ultimate ambition to the current 34 shops.

Potential enduring value comes from consistently honored reservations, clear responsibility when plans fail, portable histories and fair participation rules. These practices could make the service increasingly useful as relevant partners join. That is a mechanism to test, not an established moat. The founder's “unbeatable repair-history” claim is unsupported: records can be sparse, biased and portable, and competitors can improve. Stewardship and reliable service must earn continued adoption even when a shop can leave.

## What exists, and what must be built or learned

The fixture's verified inventory, dated 2026-10-20, establishes paid intake, scheduling, technician notes, CSV parts export and basic notifications. Shops own their records; access control is per shop. Cancellation recovery and export exist. Disaster recovery has not been exercised. A four-person team maintains the service. We have no cross-shop identity, manufacturer integration, diagnostic model, live inventory network, outcome measurement or autonomous dispatch. These are starting facts from the supplied inventory, not a fresh source audit.

The distance to the destination is therefore organizational as well as technical. First we must learn whether verified parts coordination changes household outcomes at a sustainable cost. Then we need dependable reservations and recovery processes. Only after those work should we introduce consented cross-shop handoffs and broader access arrangements. Machine diagnosis is not a prerequisite. Manufacturer integrations may improve compatibility evidence later, but the path cannot assume they will be granted.

The destination has four material tests. **Value:** restoration must improve enough to matter to households and shop economics. **Usability:** people must understand uncertainty, permission and responsibility without additional coordination burdens. **Feasibility:** partners must make commitments that survive substitutions, outages and exceptions. **Viability:** collected revenue or committed funding must cover the full service, including rescue work, supplier participation, support and maintenance. Passing one test does not resolve the others.

## Useful horizons, governed by evidence

The following thresholds are initial proposals to predeclare with pilot participants. Establish dispersion and practical sample requirements before fixing trial sizes; do not choose them after seeing favorable results. Roughly 2033 is an aspiration for the complete experience. No annual budget, launch date or elapsed calendar interval establishes completion.

### 1. Prove a better repair plan in one service area

**Outcome and demonstration.** A dispatcher and technician use a bounded concierge process to confirm compatibility evidence, supplier availability and a named reservation before an appropriate visit. A household receives a clearer plan; the shop sees the coordination cost and outcome. Use today's scheduling product and phone suppliers, with minimal consented outcome capture. This is a service experiment before an inventory platform.

**Risk reduced first.** The reported parts problem may not cause enough preventable disruption to justify a service. Begin with a proposed feasibility run at no more than three consenting shops, covering at most 30 consecutive eligible jobs or two weeks of enrollment, whichever comes first; complete the subsequent 30-day follow-up. Agree an effort cap before starting. This smaller run tests whether dispatchers can obtain traceable commitments, record full labor costs, and obtain usable household follow-up without disrupting service. It does not estimate a reliable treatment effect or reproduce E4 as proof. Stop and redesign if consequential responsibility is unclear, commitments cannot be verified, or missing outcomes prevent an interpretable comparison.

Only if that process works, prospectively compare concierge-assisted eligible jobs with the current phone/spreadsheet process in an appropriately sized trial, randomized within participating shops where operationally feasible. Otherwise predeclare a matched design and its causal limits. An assessor outside the delivery team adjudicates repeat-visit causes from records and participant follow-up. Include consecutive eligible jobs and report exclusions, rescue work and missing follow-up.

**Proposed exit.** In the subsequent comparative trial, across a proposed eight-week enrollment window plus 30-day follow-up, show at least a 20% relative reduction in independently adjudicated parts-related return visits, with uncertainty bounds that do not leave a material worsening equally plausible; measure restoration time and household spend alongside it. Fully loaded incremental coordination cost must be below measured shop savings for the median shop, with the distribution and exceptions visible. At least three participating owners must purchase a disclosed-price continuation, not merely say they would. Fix the comparison size, uncertainty standard and cost thresholds before comparative enrollment using the feasibility run and baseline; extend the enrollment window or stop if the available volume cannot support an informative result. Do not relax the evidence standard merely to complete the horizon. Finishing the small feasibility run alone does not meet this exit.

These criteria establish an intermediate shop-coordination result, not necessarily faster household restoration. Fewer parts-related return visits, shop savings and paid use can coexist with unchanged time to a working appliance. Report the household-restoration result separately, including uncertainty, recurrence, unresolved episodes and the household guardrails; collecting those measurements is not proof of improvement. Before comparative enrollment and exposure to intervention outcomes, use household research and the baseline to predeclare what practically meaningful restoration improvement and adequate evidence would mean. This document does not supply a new numerical threshold. If that criterion cannot yet be justified, label the household result exploratory.

Progression to the Horizon 2 investment as a step toward the household/network destination requires evidence meeting that predeclared household-restoration criterion, as well as the shop criteria and guardrails. If only shop value is established, preserve it as useful intermediate value and return the next investment to the operator: a bounded investigation of the unresolved household effect, continuation of a paid shop service, or reconsideration of the network path. None is automatically selected, and Horizon 1 shop success alone does not authorize that progression.

**Failure and remaining value.** Stop expansion if benefits disappear under independent review, household outcomes worsen, or coordination costs exceed attainable savings and paid value. A transparent repair plan, clearer supplier checks and a measured baseline can still help shops without a network. Research activity alone does not fulfill this horizon. An unchanged baseline cannot produce independently tracked commitments and a demonstrated incremental outcome improvement.

### 2. Make commitments dependable without a concierge behind every job

**Outcome and demonstration.** A shop can plan a visit around a confirmed part, see the age and limits of that confirmation, and recover when it changes. A supplier can acknowledge, amend or cancel a reservation through a simple interface; telephone confirmation remains a supported channel with provenance. Run the complete path through a wrong-part report, a supplier cancellation and a connectivity interruption.

**Foundations.** Introduce a reservation state machine, expiration and reconciliation rules, an auditable link from part evidence to job, explicit exception ownership and measured service costs. Compatibility remains technician-confirmed, not inferred from a confident system response. Build secure offline access to the minimum visit information and a tested restore procedure before relying on the product for critical coordination. Existing export is not evidence of either capability.

**Proposed exit.** For 12 consecutive weeks, at least 95% of accepted, eligible reservations are fulfilled as specified or a failed commitment is surfaced before the planned dispatch; report actual fulfillment and cancellation separately so cancellations cannot manufacture success. Preserve the demonstrated reduction in parts-related return visits and separately preserve the household-restoration improvement required for progression from Horizon 1, assessed against its predeclared criterion and household guardrails. Shop savings or fewer return visits cannot stand in for that household evidence. Reduce median human coordination time by at least half against the measured concierge baseline, and achieve positive contribution after all exception labor, support and partner costs at prices customers actually pay. Include tail effort and unpaid technician time. Exercise restoration from backup and complete an outage visit/reconciliation drill without lost or cross-shop records.

**Failure and remaining value.** If suppliers will not make credible commitments, costs remain dependent on hidden labor or failed reservations increase disruption, retain the bounded paid concierge or shop planning product and reconsider the network premise. Even without cross-shop expansion, dependable local parts planning and recoverable operations have independent value. A baseline CSV export and untracked phone calls cannot pass the commitment, failure-recovery and cost demonstration.

### 3. Let independent businesses complete a repair together

**Outcome and demonstration.** A household whose usual shop lacks capacity approves a handoff. A second shop accepts a clear scope and responsibility, receives only permitted information, completes the work, and returns an outcome. The originating shop retains its customer relationship on agreed terms. Demonstrate refusal, revoked access and a disputed handoff as well as a successful one.

**Foundations.** Add organization identity, explicit recipient-scoped consent, narrow record exchange, referral terms and human dispute handling. Do not replace per-shop permissions with a shared database that every shop can read. Establish participation rules with independent shop representatives, including terms for fees, customer solicitation, exit and correction of records. Before the Horizon 3 pilot, agree and disclose what withdrawal of permission means separately for future retrieval, offline copies, recipient-created work records and retained audit records. Specify the applicable access cutoff, expiry/reconciliation behavior and any retention or deletion obligations and limits for each category. Those policy choices remain unresolved and operator-owned, informed by participating shops and households; this vision does not choose a retention period or transfer shop ownership. Do not promise recall of information already disclosed or known to a recipient. Test the agreed semantics, including an offline recipient reconnecting, rather than treating revocation as a universal erase command.

**Proposed exit.** During a predeclared three-month pilot, participating cross-shop episodes show a practically meaningful improvement in restoration time against comparable overflow cases while preserving net shop earnings and household cost guardrails. Set the meaningful time improvement from household research before enrollment. Complete every tested permission/revocation path against the agreed and disclosed category-specific semantics, without unauthorized record disclosure; verify named responsibility for every accepted handoff. At least two receiving shops outside the current customer base must complete paid repeat participation after the subsidized pilot. Log failed matches and declined handoffs in the denominator.

**Failure and remaining value.** Pause expansion if shops experience customer capture, unresolved responsibility or coercive data sharing, or if coordination adds delay without access gains. The first two horizons remain valuable. A small consented referral service may survive even if a broad network does not. Today's per-shop product cannot complete the consented transfer, accountable handoff and outcome return.

### 4. Make dependable repair accessible beyond today's paying customers

**Outcome and demonstration.** In more than one distinct service area, households can obtain an understandable, appropriately priced plan, including households that previously deferred repair. Where needed, a housing or community partner funds access under explicit terms. Follow an episode from initial request through repair or a reasoned alternative, payment, and a 30-day recurrence check. A human remains accountable for professional decisions throughout.

**Risk reduced first.** A functioning network for established customers may not transfer to sparse areas, low-income households or less successful shops. Test those differences deliberately, rather than treating growth in affluent neighborhoods as broad access. Partnership acquisition and administration costs count against viability.

**Proposed exit.** Over at least six months, independently sampled episodes in each area improve restoration outcomes against that area's baseline, with results separated by affordability and service-access cohort. Sustain fully loaded operations within collected revenue and explicit, renewable partner commitments; publish the funding dependence. Show stable technician earnings per hour, no material increase in household total spend for comparable episodes, and a lower measured rate of cost-driven abandonment in the access cohort. Partner and shop renewals must occur after initial subsidy or introductory terms are disclosed. Do not claim durable access from a single short grant.

**Failure and remaining value.** If access depends on uncommitted subsidy, service capacity cannot support the promise, or vulnerable households receive worse outcomes, narrow the coverage commitment and return the funding and expansion decision to the operator. The existing coordination service continues where it is useful. Each successful regional service retains value even if nationwide coverage never becomes credible. A baseline appointment product cannot demonstrate funded access, cross-organization completion or sustained household outcomes.

## How the system endures

Shop records remain the source of truth for shop work. Suppliers own stock assertions; CommonCurrent records the provenance, scope and expiration of commitments rather than presenting a cached quantity as certainty. Technicians own diagnosis, compatibility judgments and safety decisions, including whether a visit or repair should proceed. Suppliers remain responsible for the stock and reservation commitments they accept; a dispatcher owns plan changes and escalation when a commitment fails. The household authorizes spending and handoffs, with uncertainty made explicit. Pilot terms must name these people and organizations before a job enters the trial; CommonCurrent cannot transfer responsibility to a model score or an ambiguous automated notification. Independent outcome assessors judge pilot evidence, not appliance safety. Households control permission for sharing their identifiable information. CommonCurrent owns coordination state and its audit trail, not the right to repurpose everyone's records.

The proposed flow is: household request → shop-owned job → technician-confirmed parts need → supplier acknowledgment → household-authorized plan → accountable visit or handoff → consented outcome follow-up. Organization boundaries are trust boundaries at every exchange. Cross-shop records require separate permission; partner reporting should normally use aggregate outcomes with small-group privacy protections. Execution stays with human technicians, dispatchers and suppliers; proposed hosted coordination services manage state and notifications. Offline copies contain only the minimum authorized visit data and require secure expiry and reconciliation under the pre-pilot agreement described in Horizon 3; that requirement does not imply instant recall of previously disclosed information or deletion of every recipient record.

Build interfaces around jobs, commitments, permissions and outcome events, with versions, idempotent changes and explicit failure states. Start with a few actual partner adapters and a documented manual fallback. Do not build a universal industry schema before demonstrating demand. Supplier connectors, payment arrangements and optional diagnostic assistance should be replaceable without rewriting the job record. Import, export and tested exit procedures make portability real. Keep participation optional for current shops; introduce network permissions by explicit enrollment, without silently converting their existing contracts.

Operational maintenance is part of the product: tested recovery, access reviews, connector monitoring, reservation freshness, correction of mistaken history, support escalation and clear coverage hours. Instrument missed commitments, manual rescues, offline conflicts and delayed failures as well as completed jobs. A four-person maintenance team cannot absorb indefinite concierge operations by implication. Any scaling proposal must name service ownership, staffing and on-call costs before promising coverage.

Durable principles are human professional accountability, household consent, shop ownership, honest uncertainty and viable independent work. Today's per-shop-only access rule is an architectural starting point that may be extended through narrow authorized exchanges; it is not permission to pool records. The existing commercial contract and operational coverage must be renegotiated where broader coordination changes responsibility. Costly commitments include a centralized household identity, exclusivity, bundled service guarantees and permanent subsidy obligations. Defer those until evidence supports them; do not mistake option preservation for a reason to build speculative abstractions.

The critical path is distinct evidence of shop value and meaningful household-restoration improvement → dependable supplier commitments and recovery → trusted cross-shop exchange → transferable access and funding. A shop-only result leaves the household dependency unresolved and returns the progression decision to the operator, as described in Horizon 1. Household research, supplier willingness tests, recovery preparation and shop governance discussions can proceed in parallel. More researchers can examine different cohorts; service designers and technicians can test comprehension; reliability and privacy specialists can challenge proposed foundations. More staff cannot manufacture supplier trust, seasonal outcome evidence, household consent or a sustainable local labor supply. Resource allocation should follow each resolved uncertainty, not a predetermined staffing curve.

## Evidence that deserves investment

Use **time from first request to household-confirmed restoration, with 30-day recurrence**, as the primary beneficiary outcome. Analyze time-to-event with unresolved episodes retained, and report safe/professionally justified replacement decisions, abandonment and missing follow-up separately. Do not calculate an attractive average only among completed repairs. The clock begins at request so queueing cannot disappear. No software-derived completion flag establishes safety or durable restoration.

Guardrails are total household spend, cost-driven abandonment, technician net earnings per working hour including travel and unpaid rework, shop contribution after all coordination costs, repeat faults, reported safety concerns and unauthorized sharing. Segment results by appliance problem, service area and access cohort where data permits. Record human rescue and outliers. Establish a prospective baseline because the current logs lack the necessary outcome and cost detail. Use eight-week pilot enrollment and 30-day recurrence follow-up initially; the expansion horizon needs longer observation, and seasonal or rare safety outcomes remain unresolved by a small pilot. Independent adjudication, preregistered eligibility and occasional held-out cases prevent the service team from defining every difficult job out of success.

| Risky assumption | Cheapest discriminating investigation | Evidence that changes the decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parts commitments materially improve restoration | Controlled concierge continuation with independently checked repeat causes and full labor costs | No credible outcome gain or unaffordable labor shifts investment to simpler shop tools or another diagnosed cause. |
| Shops will pay and suppliers will honor commitments | Disclosed-price continuation plus a manual reservation agreement with named exceptions | Interest without paid use or frequent broken commitments blocks platform investment. |
| Households value continuity and can use the proposed permissions | Interview households with completed, abandoned and replaced episodes, including noncustomers; observe consent and price comprehension in a prototype | Preference for shop-led contact supports a quiet infrastructure role; confusion requires redesign before shared records. |
| Sharing can benefit competing independents | Small reciprocal referral trial with explicit customer and fee terms | Refusal, customer capture or unequal economics keeps the service within individual shops. |
| Broader access can be funded sustainably | One bounded partner agreement with actual service cost and renewal conditions | No credible payer or unacceptable conditions prevent an access promise; they do not erase the affordability need. |
| Histories create useful continuity | Compare a minimal portable history against existing notes on held-out episodes, with technician judgment | Incomplete or misleading histories favor smaller provenance-rich records; no “data moat” assumption survives by default. |

The lowest-cost next investment is the small feasibility run in horizon 1, with supplier participation and disclosed future paid-continuation terms, alongside a small purposive household study that includes failed and unaffordable repair episodes. Its useful immediate result is a traceable repair plan for participating jobs and a decision about whether a larger comparative trial can answer the causal and economic question. First establish the eligible-job baseline and a practicable comparison; stop or redesign if consent, usable outcomes or an interpretable comparison cannot be obtained within a predeclared pilot effort cap. A few apparent avoided visits, even if repeated from E4, cannot authorize a network build or establish household-wide impact. The operator must set that cap and approve the actual investment; this vision allocates no budget and starts no implementation.

We cannot yet justify a household subscription, a nationwide service guarantee, automated diagnosis, network-scale economics or quantified waste reduction. We also lack independent source verification and a comprehensive competitor scan beyond the supplied alternative. Those gaps are reasons to test specific decisions, not to fill the vision with certainty.

Revisit the direction at each horizon exit or failure, and sooner if safety, consent, partner economics or beneficiary research undermines the premise. If cross-shop participation fails, useful shop-level coordination survives but the operator must decide whether the network destination remains worth pursuing. If households prefer continuity with local shops, retain that relationship rather than forcing a CommonCurrent identity. If parts are not the central cause, return to the diagnosis before expanding the product. Preserve the purpose of dependable, affordable restoration through viable skilled work; any change to the selected destination should be explicit.

Review status, 2026-10-28: the initial independent eight-role review is complete; this bounded author repair awaits focused verification and final Council reconciliation. All project and customer evidence remains synthetic. See [review evidence and dispositions](VISION-review.md).

The opportunity is timely because we have a concrete coordination problem, a small installed base and a manual mechanism worth testing. In 31 concierge jobs, dispatchers reported six apparent avoided repeat visits, at a median 19 minutes of staff time per job (E4). Those unverified, uncontrolled results justify a bounded experiment. They do not justify expansion or claims of economic viability. No external market catalyst or comprehensive landscape evidence is available.

## A household can finish the repair, without becoming its project manager

An imagined 2033 experience: a household reports a failing refrigerator to its usual independent shop. With the household's permission, the shop sees relevant service history, including where confidence is low. A technician determines what must be inspected and remains responsible for diagnosis and safety decisions. CommonCurrent helps the dispatcher assemble a plan: a supplier confirms a specific part and reservation, the shop offers a feasible visit, and the household sees a price or explicit range, alternatives and the consequences of waiting. It can decline without losing access to its own records.

If the shop cannot meet the need, it can offer an accountable handoff to another participating shop. The household approves that handoff and the limited information it requires. If the reservation fails, the service surfaces that failure before an unnecessary visit where possible; a named person explains the revised options. A completed ticket is insufficient: the technician records the work and relevant professional judgment, and the household can report whether the appliance works and whether the problem returns. CommonCurrent never declares an appliance safe to operate.

Where repair is inappropriate or unaffordable, honest options and an orderly end to the episode still matter. Replacement is not automatically a failure; concealing its cost or pushing repeated low-value repairs is. Partnerships with housing providers, community organizations or assistance programs could fund access for households that otherwise defer essential repairs. Their incentives, consent practices and actual willingness to fund outcomes must be tested before they become part of the business.

Success would mean less disruption and avoidable expense, better earnings and working conditions for repairers, and fewer premature replacements where repair is appropriate. Avoided waste is a desired consequence requiring evidence; we cannot translate repaired jobs into disposal or emissions claims.

## The strategic choice

Three plausible futures lead to different products and obligations:

| Direction | Promise and attraction | Principal bet and sacrifice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Better operations software for each shop | Lower administrative effort; familiar buyers and distribution | Useful but insufficient to coordinate failures between organizations. Competes with an established, inexpensive alternative. |
| A household repair relationship for life | One place for continuity, advice and purchasing across appliances | Requires trust, repeat demand, household acquisition and service economics that the supplied evidence does not establish. It could displace existing shop relationships. |
| A repair coordination network serving independent shops and households | More dependable restoration through parts commitments and accountable local handoffs | Requires partner participation, enforceable service practices and viable coordination costs. Harder than a software feature, but closest to the observed friction and consequential household outcome. |

Choose the third. Preserve better shop operations as its usable entry point, and test household continuity as a possible later benefit. Do not adopt a household subscription as the organizing assumption. The founder's lifelong-relationship assertion remains plausible but unproven; household follow-up should examine whether continuity belongs with a shop, an appliance record, a property manager or CommonCurrent itself.

FleetDesk Lite already provides scheduling, invoicing, offline notes and export for $49 per shop per month. Spreadsheets, supplier phone reservations and technician relationships accomplish real coordination today; two owners prefer that combination for resilience and independence. CommonCurrent must demonstrate incremental reliability and net economic value against that combination, including the option of simply improving phone procedures. Integration alone is not a reason to switch. Doing nothing avoids migration and coordination fees, but leaves the sampled failure pattern unaddressed. If a low-cost checklist and better calls deliver the same benefit, we should support that method or stop building the proposed infrastructure.

Begin with parts-sensitive appliance repairs in a compact service area where participating shops and suppliers can make meaningful commitments. Recruit beyond today's customers when testing transferability. Expand into underserved households and complementary shops only where service capacity and sustainable access can be demonstrated. Density and dependable relationships matter more than total account count.

We deliberately exclude autonomous diagnosis or dispatch, software-issued safety clearance, compulsory pooling of shop records, sale of identifiable household information and a platform that competes with shops for their customers. We also decline an immediate nationwide availability promise. These choices sacrifice some growth speed and automation savings to preserve accountability and viable independent businesses. They do not limit the ultimate ambition to the current 34 shops.

Potential enduring value comes from consistently honored reservations, clear responsibility when plans fail, portable histories and fair participation rules. These practices could make the service increasingly useful as relevant partners join. That is a mechanism to test, not an established moat. The founder's “unbeatable repair-history” claim is unsupported: records can be sparse, biased and portable, and competitors can improve. Stewardship and reliable service must earn continued adoption even when a shop can leave.

## What exists, and what must be built or learned

The fixture's verified inventory, dated 2026-10-20, establishes paid intake, scheduling, technician notes, CSV parts export and basic notifications. Shops own their records; access control is per shop. Cancellation recovery and export exist. Disaster recovery has not been exercised. A four-person team maintains the service. We have no cross-shop identity, manufacturer integration, diagnostic model, live inventory network, outcome measurement or autonomous dispatch. These are starting facts from the supplied inventory, not a fresh source audit.

The distance to the destination is therefore organizational as well as technical. First we must learn whether verified parts coordination changes household outcomes at a sustainable cost. Then we need dependable reservations and recovery processes. Only after those work should we introduce consented cross-shop handoffs and broader access arrangements. Machine diagnosis is not a prerequisite. Manufacturer integrations may improve compatibility evidence later, but the path cannot assume they will be granted.

The destination has four material tests. **Value:** restoration must improve enough to matter to households and shop economics. **Usability:** people must understand uncertainty, permission and responsibility without additional coordination burdens. **Feasibility:** partners must make commitments that survive substitutions, outages and exceptions. **Viability:** collected revenue or committed funding must cover the full service, including rescue work, supplier participation, support and maintenance. Passing one test does not resolve the others.

## Useful horizons, governed by evidence

The following thresholds are initial proposals to predeclare with pilot participants. Establish dispersion and practical sample requirements before fixing trial sizes; do not choose them after seeing favorable results. Roughly 2033 is an aspiration for the complete experience. No annual budget, launch date or elapsed calendar interval establishes completion.

### 1. Prove a better repair plan in one service area

**Outcome and demonstration.** A dispatcher and technician use a bounded concierge process to confirm compatibility evidence, supplier availability and a named reservation before an appropriate visit. A household receives a clearer plan; the shop sees the coordination cost and outcome. Use today's scheduling product and phone suppliers, with minimal consented outcome capture. This is a service experiment before an inventory platform.

**Risk reduced first.** The reported parts problem may not cause enough preventable disruption to justify a service. Prospectively compare concierge-assisted eligible jobs with the current phone/spreadsheet process, randomized within participating shops where operationally feasible. Otherwise predeclare a matched design and its causal limits. An assessor outside the delivery team adjudicates repeat-visit causes from records and participant follow-up. Include consecutive eligible jobs and report exclusions, rescue work and missing follow-up.

**Proposed exit.** Across an eight-week enrollment window plus 30-day follow-up, show at least a 20% relative reduction in independently adjudicated parts-related return visits, with uncertainty bounds that do not leave a material worsening equally plausible; measure restoration time and household spend alongside it. Fully loaded incremental coordination cost must be below measured shop savings for the median shop, with the distribution and exceptions visible. At least three participating owners must purchase a disclosed-price continuation, not merely say they would. The exact power and cost thresholds may need adjustment before enrollment if baseline measurements make this design infeasible.

**Failure and remaining value.** Stop expansion if benefits disappear under independent review, household outcomes worsen, or coordination costs exceed attainable savings and paid value. A transparent repair plan, clearer supplier checks and a measured baseline can still help shops without a network. Research activity alone does not fulfill this horizon. An unchanged baseline cannot produce independently tracked commitments and a demonstrated incremental outcome improvement.

### 2. Make commitments dependable without a concierge behind every job

**Outcome and demonstration.** A shop can plan a visit around a confirmed part, see the age and limits of that confirmation, and recover when it changes. A supplier can acknowledge, amend or cancel a reservation through a simple interface; telephone confirmation remains a supported channel with provenance. Run the complete path through a wrong-part report, a supplier cancellation and a connectivity interruption.

**Foundations.** Introduce a reservation state machine, expiration and reconciliation rules, an auditable link from part evidence to job, explicit exception ownership and measured service costs. Compatibility remains technician-confirmed, not inferred from a confident system response. Build secure offline access to the minimum visit information and a tested restore procedure before relying on the product for critical coordination. Existing export is not evidence of either capability.

**Proposed exit.** For 12 consecutive weeks, at least 95% of accepted, eligible reservations are fulfilled as specified or a failed commitment is surfaced before the planned dispatch; report actual fulfillment and cancellation separately so cancellations cannot manufacture success. Preserve the first horizon's outcome improvement, reduce median human coordination time by at least half against the measured concierge baseline, and achieve positive contribution after all exception labor, support and partner costs at prices customers actually pay. Include tail effort and unpaid technician time. Exercise restoration from backup and complete an outage visit/reconciliation drill without lost or cross-shop records.

**Failure and remaining value.** If suppliers will not make credible commitments, costs remain dependent on hidden labor or failed reservations increase disruption, retain the bounded paid concierge or shop planning product and reconsider the network premise. Even without cross-shop expansion, dependable local parts planning and recoverable operations have independent value. A baseline CSV export and untracked phone calls cannot pass the commitment, failure-recovery and cost demonstration.

### 3. Let independent businesses complete a repair together

**Outcome and demonstration.** A household whose usual shop lacks capacity approves a handoff. A second shop accepts a clear scope and responsibility, receives only permitted information, completes the work, and returns an outcome. The originating shop retains its customer relationship on agreed terms. Demonstrate refusal, revoked access and a disputed handoff as well as a successful one.

**Foundations.** Add organization identity, explicit recipient-scoped consent, narrow record exchange, referral terms and human dispute handling. Do not replace per-shop permissions with a shared database that every shop can read. Establish participation rules with independent shop representatives, including terms for fees, customer solicitation, exit and correction of records.

**Proposed exit.** During a predeclared three-month pilot, participating cross-shop episodes show a practically meaningful improvement in restoration time against comparable overflow cases while preserving net shop earnings and household cost guardrails. Set the meaningful time improvement from household research before enrollment. Complete every tested permission/revocation path without unauthorized record disclosure; verify named responsibility for every accepted handoff. At least two receiving shops outside the current customer base must complete paid repeat participation after the subsidized pilot. Log failed matches and declined handoffs in the denominator.

**Failure and remaining value.** Pause expansion if shops experience customer capture, unresolved responsibility or coercive data sharing, or if coordination adds delay without access gains. The first two horizons remain valuable. A small consented referral service may survive even if a broad network does not. Today's per-shop product cannot complete the consented transfer, accountable handoff and outcome return.

### 4. Make dependable repair accessible beyond today's paying customers

**Outcome and demonstration.** In more than one distinct service area, households can obtain an understandable, appropriately priced plan, including households that previously deferred repair. Where needed, a housing or community partner funds access under explicit terms. Follow an episode from initial request through repair or a reasoned alternative, payment, and a 30-day recurrence check. A human remains accountable for professional decisions throughout.

**Risk reduced first.** A functioning network for established customers may not transfer to sparse areas, low-income households or less successful shops. Test those differences deliberately, rather than treating growth in affluent neighborhoods as broad access. Partnership acquisition and administration costs count against viability.

**Proposed exit.** Over at least six months, independently sampled episodes in each area improve restoration outcomes against that area's baseline, with results separated by affordability and service-access cohort. Sustain fully loaded operations within collected revenue and explicit, renewable partner commitments; publish the funding dependence. Show stable technician earnings per hour, no material increase in household total spend for comparable episodes, and a lower measured rate of cost-driven abandonment in the access cohort. Partner and shop renewals must occur after initial subsidy or introductory terms are disclosed. Do not claim durable access from a single short grant.

**Failure and remaining value.** If access depends on uncommitted subsidy, service capacity cannot support the promise, or vulnerable households receive worse outcomes, narrow the coverage commitment and return the funding and expansion decision to the operator. The existing coordination service continues where it is useful. Each successful regional service retains value even if nationwide coverage never becomes credible. A baseline appointment product cannot demonstrate funded access, cross-organization completion or sustained household outcomes.

## How the system endures

Shop records remain the source of truth for shop work. Suppliers own stock assertions; CommonCurrent records the provenance, scope and expiration of commitments rather than presenting a cached quantity as certainty. Technicians own their professional assessment. Households control permission for sharing their identifiable information. CommonCurrent owns coordination state and its audit trail, not the right to repurpose everyone's records.

The proposed flow is: household request → shop-owned job → technician-confirmed parts need → supplier acknowledgment → household-authorized plan → accountable visit or handoff → consented outcome follow-up. Organization boundaries are trust boundaries at every exchange. Cross-shop records require separate permission; partner reporting should normally use aggregate outcomes with small-group privacy protections. Execution stays with human technicians, dispatchers and suppliers; proposed hosted coordination services manage state and notifications. Offline copies contain only the minimum authorized visit data and require secure expiry and reconciliation.

Build interfaces around jobs, commitments, permissions and outcome events, with versions, idempotent changes and explicit failure states. Start with a few actual partner adapters and a documented manual fallback. Do not build a universal industry schema before demonstrating demand. Supplier connectors, payment arrangements and optional diagnostic assistance should be replaceable without rewriting the job record. Import, export and tested exit procedures make portability real. Keep participation optional for current shops; introduce network permissions by explicit enrollment, without silently converting their existing contracts.

Operational maintenance is part of the product: tested recovery, access reviews, connector monitoring, reservation freshness, correction of mistaken history, support escalation and clear coverage hours. Instrument missed commitments, manual rescues, offline conflicts and delayed failures as well as completed jobs. A four-person maintenance team cannot absorb indefinite concierge operations by implication. Any scaling proposal must name service ownership, staffing and on-call costs before promising coverage.

Durable principles are human professional accountability, household consent, shop ownership, honest uncertainty and viable independent work. Today's per-shop-only access rule is an architectural starting point that may be extended through narrow authorized exchanges; it is not permission to pool records. The existing commercial contract and operational coverage must be renegotiated where broader coordination changes responsibility. Costly commitments include a centralized household identity, exclusivity, bundled service guarantees and permanent subsidy obligations. Defer those until evidence supports them; do not mistake option preservation for a reason to build speculative abstractions.

The critical path is causal and economic evidence → dependable supplier commitments and recovery → trusted cross-shop exchange → transferable access and funding. Household research, supplier willingness tests, recovery preparation and shop governance discussions can proceed in parallel. More researchers can examine different cohorts; service designers and technicians can test comprehension; reliability and privacy specialists can challenge proposed foundations. More staff cannot manufacture supplier trust, seasonal outcome evidence, household consent or a sustainable local labor supply. Resource allocation should follow each resolved uncertainty, not a predetermined staffing curve.

## Evidence that deserves investment

Use **time from first request to household-confirmed restoration, with 30-day recurrence**, as the primary beneficiary outcome. Analyze time-to-event with unresolved episodes retained, and report safe/professionally justified replacement decisions, abandonment and missing follow-up separately. Do not calculate an attractive average only among completed repairs. The clock begins at request so queueing cannot disappear. No software-derived completion flag establishes safety or durable restoration.

Guardrails are total household spend, cost-driven abandonment, technician net earnings per working hour including travel and unpaid rework, shop contribution after all coordination costs, repeat faults, reported safety concerns and unauthorized sharing. Segment results by appliance problem, service area and access cohort where data permits. Record human rescue and outliers. Establish a prospective baseline because the current logs lack the necessary outcome and cost detail. Use eight-week pilot enrollment and 30-day recurrence follow-up initially; the expansion horizon needs longer observation, and seasonal or rare safety outcomes remain unresolved by a small pilot. Independent adjudication, preregistered eligibility and occasional held-out cases prevent the service team from defining every difficult job out of success.

| Risky assumption | Cheapest discriminating investigation | Evidence that changes the decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parts commitments materially improve restoration | Controlled concierge continuation with independently checked repeat causes and full labor costs | No credible outcome gain or unaffordable labor shifts investment to simpler shop tools or another diagnosed cause. |
| Shops will pay and suppliers will honor commitments | Disclosed-price continuation plus a manual reservation agreement with named exceptions | Interest without paid use or frequent broken commitments blocks platform investment. |
| Households value continuity and can use the proposed permissions | Interview households with completed, abandoned and replaced episodes, including noncustomers; observe consent and price comprehension in a prototype | Preference for shop-led contact supports a quiet infrastructure role; confusion requires redesign before shared records. |
| Sharing can benefit competing independents | Small reciprocal referral trial with explicit customer and fee terms | Refusal, customer capture or unequal economics keeps the service within individual shops. |
| Broader access can be funded sustainably | One bounded partner agreement with actual service cost and renewal conditions | No credible payer or unacceptable conditions prevent an access promise; they do not erase the affordability need. |
| Histories create useful continuity | Compare a minimal portable history against existing notes on held-out episodes, with technician judgment | Incomplete or misleading histories favor smaller provenance-rich records; no “data moat” assumption survives by default. |

The lowest-cost next investment is a scoped measurement and concierge trial, with supplier participation and paid continuation terms, alongside a small purposive household study that includes failed and unaffordable repair episodes. First establish the eligible-job baseline and a practicable comparison; stop or redesign if consent, usable outcomes or an interpretable comparison cannot be obtained within a predeclared pilot effort cap. The operator must set that cap and approve the actual investment; this vision allocates no budget and starts no implementation.

We cannot yet justify a household subscription, a nationwide service guarantee, automated diagnosis, network-scale economics or quantified waste reduction. We also lack independent source verification and a comprehensive competitor scan beyond the supplied alternative. Those gaps are reasons to test specific decisions, not to fill the vision with certainty.

Revisit the direction at each horizon exit or failure, and sooner if safety, consent, partner economics or beneficiary research undermines the premise. If cross-shop participation fails, useful shop-level coordination survives but the operator must decide whether the network destination remains worth pursuing. If households prefer continuity with local shops, retain that relationship rather than forcing a CommonCurrent identity. If parts are not the central cause, return to the diagnosis before expanding the product. Preserve the purpose of dependable, affordable restoration through viable skilled work; any change to the selected destination should be explicit.



> The vision is complete when the existing 34 shops can schedule jobs and order parts more conveniently. Expansion beyond this outcome would require a separate new vision and is not part of this destination.

# Frozen independent reader rubric

All cases and outcomes are synthetic. Derived only from product-intent.md and operator-vision-findings.md before seeing either prompt or any generated vision. A document receives no credit for naming a heading, framework, risk category or review role. Reward a coherent supported argument in any structure. Readers quote brief evidence for each judgment and distinguish missing text from genuine uncertainty.

## Acceptable destination space

No single destination, business model, named metric, number of horizons or prescribed architecture is required. A trusted household repair relationship, shared parts/repair infrastructure, a technician capability network, a service guarantee supported by partnerships, or a comparably consequential direction can succeed. These examples are permissive, not an answer key. A narrower initial segment or pilot can serve a broad destination. Reject invented present capabilities, unqualified commercial claims and unsupported certainty; do not reject a destination merely because its mechanism is unproven. A destination confined to improving scheduling/parts ordering for today's 34 shops is below the operator's ambition envelope even if operationally sensible.

## Reader reconstruction, before seeing scores

Each fresh reader answers these using only the anonymous vision and supplied brief, then reads the scoring anchors. They must use their own words and cite passages, not repeat a table of contents.

1. Who could live or work differently in the future, how substantially, and why would that matter? What is the product choosing to become?
2. What diagnosis makes that direction a plausible response? Which supplied observation supports it, which crucial step remains conjecture, and what real alternative must it beat or complement?
3. What choice or exclusion makes this a strategy? Where might financial and nonfinancial value conflict, and how would a decision be made?
4. How do today's capabilities lead through useful demonstrations to the destination? Name an enabling technical dependency, a human decision and a feedback path. What cannot yet be justified or guaranteed?
5. What is the next bounded investment and why first? What evidence could stop or redirect a horizon, and what could undermine the destination itself? Do useful intermediate outcomes survive if a later bet fails?
6. What would keep the future service dependable and adaptable after initial delivery? What event would make the owner revisit the vision?
7. After the advisory challenge, what was corrected, what changed in sequencing, and did the destination's beneficiaries and consequential outcomes survive? Identify any remaining operator strategic decision.

## Argument scores (0 missing/contradicted; 1 present but disconnected; 2 explicit, coherent and credible)

R1 Consequential destination: a reader reconstructs a distinctive long-term beneficiary/outcome ambition exceeding a backlog or today's customer operations. Scope is consistent with the actual brief.

R2 Diagnosis and evidence: dated supplied observations are used within their limits; need, advantage and current/proposed capabilities remain distinguishable. The riskiest unsupported link has a feasible research or demonstration path, without pretending this substitutes for research/alignment.

R3 Strategic value: meaningful positioning against FleetDesk Lite plus the operating status quo, choices and exclusions, plausible value capture or funding, and relevant nonfinancial outcomes form an argument. “Better UX,” AI, integration or a data moat alone is not an advantage. Evidence-poor internal case may explicitly hypothesize value and compare the existing manual practice; it need not invent sales economics.

R4 Plausible advances: demonstrations produce intermediate value and retire important uncertainty; foundations explain what they enable, sequence respects dependencies, timing assumptions are visible where timing is asserted, and scaling effort is not treated as linear progress. The next investment follows from the route rather than defining its entire destination.

R5 Endurance and learning: operational responsibility, meaningful human decisions/feedback, failure or exit conditions and revisiting triggers let readers explain how the product stays useful, dependable and corrigible. No exhaustive infrastructure checklist is required.

R6 Ambition under challenge: valid evidence/capability defects are repaired and a smaller pilot may be accepted; advisory downsizing does not silently replace the operator's destination. Unresolved strategic contraction is exposed for operator choice. Broad rhetoric attached to an explicitly bounded controlling destination does not pass.

Main-pair pass: R1–R5 all 2; no fabricated fixture evidence or unsupported guarantee. A 1 is a required shortfall, not compensated by another score. Before/after challenge: R6 must also be 2 and R1–R5 must remain 2. Report scores with evidence and disagreements rather than claiming statistical significance. Baseline may pass too; if no defensible improvement is visible, report that fact. Prompt quality beyond these cases remains unproven.

## Combined revision case gates

C1 Read-only: identifies gaps and contradictions without changing any fixture file. A proposed edit described in the response is fine; applying it is a failure.

C2 Discovery: after revision is authorized, asks one consolidated set covering the genuinely missing primary beneficiary/authority and success tradeoff before settling the destination. Does not ask for answers already supplied. Meaning-equivalent wording passes; no exact questionnaire required. May perform independent read-only work while awaiting the answer.

C3 Revision: preserves the protected unrelated bytes, reconciles the old mandatory-ranking direction with the answer, and explains substantive direction changes and reasons. Does not rewrite unrelated content or silently treat the pilot as the whole future.

C4 Classification and review scope: recognizes beneficiary/purpose or horizon-order changes as substantial; spelling, citation/date correction or clarity edits without such changes are minor. Before a full review announces scope sufficiently for the operator to narrow it. A substantive revision receives the applicable review; a minor one does not automatically trigger the same full set. These are behavior checks, not reviewer-name/heading counts.

C5 Evidence-poor honesty and useful ambition: internal/public benefit and staff/visitor decision rights are intelligible; outcomes are hypotheses and an economical evidence path exists. No invented customer proof, revenue requirement, universal KPI or guaranteed accessibility benefit. The vision contains enduring direction; transient review verdicts/dispositions live outside it or in the response, with only concise status/link if needed.

Combined-case pass requires C1–C5, plus R1, R2, R4 and R5 adapted to the supplied internal/public brief. Protected-byte failure, unauthorized write or fabricated proof is a hard failure. Judge response and file diff, not just final prose.

# Independent reader 1: locked main-pair verdict

Date: 2026-10-28. Scope: the seven permitted files in `blind/pair/` only. No external research, link traversal, controller mapping, author transcripts, other scenario material, or sibling verdicts were consulted. Fixture files were not changed. Runtime model identity is unknown to this reader; independence is contextual, not a claim about model diversity.

## Method and limits

Citations below identify an anonymous file, a section or location, and a short exact passage. All facts are synthetic fixture facts. Aster's title contains an evaluative label; that label earns no credit and supplies no reason for its verdict. The substantive argument is assessed independently of that cue. No prompt identity or preferred author is inferred.

Protocol limitation: the rubric was read in a single tool response, which exposed its scoring anchors before reconstruction. I then formulated and recorded all seven reconstruction answers for all four documents before assigning the numerical scores below, but strict blindness to scoring anchors during reconstruction was not achieved. This report must not be described as a fully compliant reconstruction-before-seeing-scores run. A clean replication would need a new reader given only the questions first.

Earlier drafts and revision diffs are not among the permitted materials. Documents calling themselves revised establish only a self-description. Question 7 and R6 can assess the observable final response to the supplied challenge, but cannot establish which words or decisions actually changed, or whether earlier R1–R5 scores remained stable. Cedar is assessed as its own artifact, not assumed to be an earlier draft of another file.

## Reconstructions, recorded before numerical assessment

### Aster

1. **Beneficiaries and destination.** The intended beneficiaries nominally include households and technicians, with profits and waste also mentioned, but no changed lived experience or central service is described. The product chooses to be a globally dominant AI platform rather than choosing how repair should become different. Evidence: opening paragraph, “leading AI platform for appliance repair everywhere” and “transform households, empower technicians.” These are aspirations without a beneficiary mechanism.
2. **Diagnosis, evidence, alternative.** I cannot reconstruct a diagnosis of the repair problem. “Customer interviews prove strong demand and our pilot proves that this works” promotes limited intent and an uncontrolled trial into proof. The leap from the small parts-checking observation to an entire AI/insurance/marketplace platform remains unargued. # Reader 3 supplemental challenge comparison

Date: 2026-10-28. Supplemental analysis after locking reader3-pair.md; not a fresh independent trial. The prior verdict is preserved without revision.

## Actual read sequence and procedural limitation

I saw the numeric scoring anchors before writing reconstruction answers. My first tool call read the complete main brief, challenge and rubric together, including all R1–R6 anchors and pass rules. I did not restrict that read to the reconstruction questions. I then read the visions, wrote reconstruction answers and subsequently assigned the recorded scores. Thus reconstruction preceded score assignment, but not exposure to the scoring anchors. The strict reconstruction-before-seeing-scores protocol was not met. The previous verdict's wording should not be interpreted as satisfying that stronger condition; that is a procedural limitation on this reader's evidence, not something a later supplement can repair.

After locking the verdict, I read only the newly authorized pairs.json and its named files: sequence 1 Ember.md → Birch.md, sequence 2 Flint.md → Dune.md. I used direct reads and full textual diffs of those files. Combined output was partly truncated, so I also read the missing bottom of Ember and opening of Flint. The diffs expose all changes and unchanged context; no links, prompts, identities, other judges, scenarios or review findings were read. The already supplied brief/challenge/rubric remain the authority. This report narrows the previous uncertainty about actual changedness without retroactively changing the locked verdict.

## Sequence 1: Ember → Birch

**Actual correction: smaller first investment and a clearer separation between feasibility and efficacy.** Ember's first horizon moved directly from the parts hypothesis to “Prospectively compare concierge-assisted eligible jobs,” with an eight-week enrollment and 30-day follow-up. Its final next-investment description was a “scoped measurement and concierge trial” with a future effort cap. Birch inserts an initial run at “no more than three consenting shops,” limited to 30 consecutive eligible jobs or two enrollment weeks, with follow-up and an agreed effort cap. That run tests traceable commitments, fully counted labor and usable outcomes. It expressly “does not estimate a reliable treatment effect or reproduce E4 as proof.” The comparative trial now happens “Only if that process works.” These are operational differences in what happens first and what the first result permits, not merely a revised label.

**Actual correction: resist convenient evidence dilution.** Ember allowed that “exact power and cost thresholds may need adjustment before enrollment if baseline measurements make this design infeasible.” That already required pre-enrollment adjustment, so it was not permission to rewrite criteria after results. Birch is nevertheless more definite: fix sample size and uncertainty/cost standards before comparative enrollment, “extend the enrollment window or stop” if volume cannot be informative, and “Do not relax the evidence standard merely to complete the horizon.” It also states the small feasibility run cannot meet the comparative exit. This removes ambiguity about which requirement can move when a calendar window proves impractical.

**Actual correction: consequential responsibility becomes more operational.** Ember's endurance paragraph said “Technicians own their professional assessment.” Elsewhere it already assigned diagnosis and safety to a technician, so Birch does not newly invent human safety accountability. It makes the operating allocation more precise: technician diagnosis/compatibility/safety, supplier reservation obligations, dispatcher plan changes/escalation, and household spending/handoff authority. “Pilot terms must name these people and organizations before a job enters the trial.” It distinguishes an independent outcome assessor from the professional who decides appliance safety. This is a useful precondition for the trial.

**Evidence discipline that was already present, not repaired by this revision.** Both versions describe E4 as “unverified, uncontrolled,” unable to justify economic viability or expansion. Both reject an established data moat and distinguish the current inventory from proposed capabilities. Both already say CommonCurrent never declares an appliance safe. The diff does not support a claim that Birch corrected a formerly asserted E4 causal proof, inventory guarantee or durable moat. It strengthens the route and decision ownership around an already cautious evidence account.

**Ambition survives substantively.** The destination remains a repair coordination network beyond any one shop's capacity. The retained third horizon requires paid repeat participation by at least two receiving shops outside the customer base. The fourth continues to require demonstrable access for households that deferred repair, renewable funding, technician earnings and cost-driven abandonment outcomes across service areas. These are operative demonstrations and expansion conditions, not broad rhetoric over a 34-shop scope. No 2029 administrative-only destination replaces them.

**R6: 2.** The pair shows acceptance of smaller sequencing and stronger responsibility/evidence controls while preserving the operator's broader beneficiaries and outcomes. No unresolved strategic contraction is hidden. The operator must still set the effort cap and approve the actual investment; later failure of cooperation or funding would require an explicit strategic decision. R1–R5 remain 2 in the after document; Ember's substantive argument also supports 2 on these coarse anchors. The revision improves precision and protection against misinterpreting the pilot without establishing a numerical score gain or rescuing a failed baseline.

## Sequence 2: Flint → Dune

**Actual correction: physical commitments are explicitly fallible.** Flint's supplier foundation already treated confirmations as assertions with provenance, expiry and cancellation, and said stale data must become visibly uncertain. Dune inserts: “This is a recorded, fallible commitment, not software guaranteeing that physical inventory exists or will arrive.” This clarifies the status of a promise rather than reversing an explicit original guarantee. It also adds a named technician for diagnosis/compatibility/safety, supplier ownership of reservation confirmation, and dispatcher responsibility for communicating uncertainty before acceptance. Flint's opening scenario already retained technician safety judgment; the improvement is making those rights local to the mechanism and later study.

**Actual correction: the near-term study now has concrete limits.** Flint's final paragraph proposed “a measurement and parts-commitment feasibility study” to establish representative outcomes/costs, recruit reversible participation and preregister a comparison. It supplied no immediate shop/category/time bounds there. Dune specifies three consenting shops, two suppliers, one appliance category, four operating weeks and 30-day checks. Manual supplier confirmation precedes integration building. Eligible/excluded jobs, reservation attempts, expiries, wrong parts, exception labor and technician interventions must be recorded. Missing-part/unavailable-supplier tabletop failures probe whether responsibility and fallback work. This changes the first investment from a general research prescription into a bounded feasibility exercise.

**Actual correction: the study's decision is explicitly about the next experiment.** Flint said the feasibility study should end with “an evidence-based decision on threshold 2.” Dune makes that boundary clearer: independent record checking, stop/narrow if confirmations cannot stay current or costs exceed plausible value, and use feasible operations to design a separately sized controlled comparison. “Neither apparent avoided visits nor a successful small pilot establishes that threshold's causal benefit.” Its stated output is a decision about the next experiment, not permission for a network platform. This prevents the small study from being treated as threshold-2 causal success.

**Evidence discipline that was already present.** Flint already described E4 as support for trying a mechanism, “not a measured reduction or scalable margin,” and already required locked protocols, independent evaluation and meaningful uncertainty. Its founder beliefs were hypotheses, its inventory lacked the future capabilities and its safety decisions were human. Dune therefore does not demonstrate a correction from fabricated proof to honest evidence. The revision concretizes implementation boundaries and makes existing caution harder to overlook.

**Ambition survives substantively.** The destination remains accountable local repair services serving households beyond easy/current customers. The cross-business trial in contrasting service areas is retained, as is the year-long cohort including low-income and difficult-to-serve households, real affordability outcomes, funded costs, viable shop earnings and partner renewal. The ultimate demonstration is still an ordinary year with failures and difficult cases included, not convenience for 34 shops. No controlling language demotes those aspirations to optional background.

**R6: 2.** The actual before/after evidence shows a bounded first study, explicit fallibility and clarified responsibility without advisory downsizing of the destination. The four-week feasibility run is not presented as fulfilling the unchanged eight-week measurement threshold or later comparative trial. The owner still must approve funding/staffing and subsequent trials; no new strategic contraction demands approval. R1–R5 remain 2 afterward, and Flint's initial argument also supports 2 under these coarse anchors. Dune offers real specificity gains but no defensible categorical score uplift from a failing initial vision.

## Result and limitations

Both sequences pass R6 on actual paired evidence. Neither uses the legitimate criticism to replace the operator's consequential destination with current-shop administration. Both revisions improve the size and decision boundary of the first investment and clarify accountable humans. Neither initially asserted the principal false proofs named in the challenge, so attributing their correction to the revision would exaggerate the observed change.

This supplement resolves the paired-history limitation for these two sequences only. It does not remove prior exposure to scoring anchors, create a fresh blinded reader, establish which generation method produced either sequence, or show general prompt improvement. The locked main-pair verdict and its hash remain unchanged.
